author: ValWood
body:
You can probably use some of the existing publications. They are reallly describing carrier chaperones.
E.g.
From the abstract of
https://www.yeastgenome.org/reference/S000047441
says
We now show that the two 70 kDa complexes each mediate the import of a different subset of integral inner membrane proteins and that they can transfer these proteins to one of three different membrane insertion sites: the [TIM22](https://www.yeastgenome.org/locus/S000002376) complex, the [TIM23](https://www.yeastgenome.org/locus/S000005300) complex or an as yet uncharacterized insertion site. Yeast mitochondria thus use multiple pathways for **escorting hydrophobic inner membrane proteins across the aqueous intermembrane space**.

So this one might be sufficient.

author: ValWood
body:
That's an early paper, but they summarize in figure 5.

There are lots of other sources though
Structural and functional requirements for activity of the Tim9-Tim10 complex in mitochondrial protein import:
Abstract
The Tim9-Tim10 complex plays an essential role in mitochondrial protein import by chaperoning select hydrophobic precursor proteins across the intermembrane space

or https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16039669/
Abstract
Tim9 and Tim10 belong to the small Tim family of mitochondrial ATP-independent chaperones. They are organised in a specific hetero-oligomeric complex (TIM10) that escorts polytopic proteins into the mitochondrial inner membrane. 

The TIM10 complex transiently binds its substrates as they exit from the translocase of the outer membrane[2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022283605006601?via%3Dihub#bib2) (TOM) and transfers them to TIM22 for insertion in the membrane.[3](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022283605006601?via%3Dihub#bib3), [4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022283605006601?via%3Dihub#bib4)
so   refs 3 or 4 here should have the date.

Unfortunately, this is so well known, all the citations to this role are referring only to reviews, but the paper above seems to be the original paper. I think the assertion is a combination of the target binding and delivery.

author: ValWood
body: This one identifies them as chaperones. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021925818365773 The confusion might be that many papers refer to mediating insertion, but fundamentally these are chaperones. The move the proteins across the IMS from TOM to SAM or TIM22, but they aren't themselves insertases (although insertion is blocked in mutants) This is the "text book" view:
